newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK Q4 GDP will not trigger rate rise.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK Q4 GDP will not trigger rate rise.

text.p: Fourth quarter UK GDP data due on Monday are set to show the economy grew steadily towards the end of last year, but not by enough to prod Chancellor Kenneth Clarke into raising rates before the election, analysts say.
The Reuters consensus suggests GDP grew 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter, faster than 0.7 percent in the third, pushing year-on-year growth up to 2.6 percent compared with 2.4 percent.
"The prospect of a pre-election rate rise swings almost exclusively on this number," said Adam Cole, UK economist at James Capel.
Both Clarke and Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George placed great emphasis on GDP nearing the trend rate of growth in the third quarter when they raised rates on October 30.

This is the last period for which the authorities will get GDP figures before the election, which must be held by May. Second quarter GDP figures will not be available until April when the election will either be over, or the campaign in full swing.
Barring any major surprises from Monday's data, most analysts expect Clarke will withstand pressure from George and keep rates on hold.
They said weakness in the manufacturing sector was more than offset by higher energy output and buoyant services growth in the period, allowing overall activity to accelerate.

"Although manufacturing output appears to have risen at a slower pace than in the third quarter, overall industrial production has been supported by increases in energy output, and service sector output remains healthy," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
He forecasts growth in line with the consensus.
Cole's forecast is well below the consensus at 0.6 percent in the quarter for a year-on-year rate of 2.4 percent.
"Growth will reined back by weak industrial production and a sharp fall in production and agricultural output," he said.
Agricultural output raced ahead in the third quarter due to the early harvest, and is in for a correction in the fourth.

Philip Shaw, group economist at Union Plc, agreed agricultural slowdown dampened growth. "Q3 figures were boosted by an unusually large 7.0 percent rise in agriculture which we doubt will be repeated in the fourth quarter."
He said a slowdown in manufacturing growth will also restrain expansion overall.
"However, we expect continued buoyancy in the service sector and greater signs of life in the construction sector given the recent upturn in housing starts."
But most economists said even if GDP is slightly above forecasts and excedes the trend rate of 2.5 percent or so, Clarke will still feel he has a good case to overrule George and keep rates on hold.
The Chancellor cited the strength of sterling, which dampens inflation by making imported goods cheaper, as a key factor behind his decision not to raise rates in January.
"The continued surge in the pound has since overtaken the pace of economic expansion as a key factor in deciding the stance of monetary policy," said Shaw.
